title: Contouring mitigates voiding at the lithium/ceramic electrolyte interface on discharging solid-state batteries - Nature Energy
text:
Download PDF

AbstractInterfacial void formation during discharge limits the practical performance of lithium metal solid-state batteries. Here we show that introducing an egg-box topography at the Li/Li6PS5Cl interface increases the discharge current at which voiding commences tenfold, from 0.2 to 2 mA cm−2 at 2 MPa and 30 °C. The contoured interface also sustains pulsed currents up to 3 mA cm−2 at 30 °C and 8 mA cm−2 at 60 °C without cell failure. Under these conditions, it does not completely eliminate void formation but suppresses void growth and associated voltage polarization. Consequently, it sustains discharge profiles derived from the Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Procedure, representing realistic electric vehicle driving demands, whereas non-contoured interfaces fail rapidly. A full cell with a thin contoured solid electrolyte retains this advantage over its non-contoured counterpart. Contouring the Li/solid electrolyte interface is therefore an effective strategy for enabling practically relevant discharge rates in solid-state batteries.

Batteries

Lithium-Ion Battery Technologies and Applications

MainVoids can form at the lithium/ceramic electrolyte interface during the discharge of solid-state batteries, leading to increased polarization and ultimately cell failure1,2. Voiding occurs when the flux of Li+ away from the interface through the solid electrolyte exceeds the rate at which Li can be transported to the interface within the anode3,4,5. Because of the resulting reduction in contact area, leading to increased local current density during subsequent charging6,7, voiding can also initiate dendrite formation at lower charging currents, ultimately leading to short circuit and cell failure8,9,10. The recognition of this fact has led to considerable focus on the voiding problem in recent years11,12,13,14,15.Voiding can be alleviated to some extent by applying a sufficiently high stack pressure (for example, >10 MPa) such that the creep rate of lithium is enough to match the discharge current density16,17. However, practical solid-state batteries are very unlikely to operate at such high stack pressures; typically, ≤2 MPa will be required. The challenge is how to mitigate voiding at practical discharge currents without high pressures. To date, approaches have included: forming lithium-based alloys in an attempt to access higher Li transport rates within the anode18,19,20,21,22, the introduction of interlayers between the lithium metal and the ceramic electrolyte, again to improve Li mass transport to the interface23,24,25,26, and the formation of 3D architectures of mixed ionic- and electronic- conductors within the anode27,28.An alternative, which requires no new materials, alloys or interlayers, is to contour the interface, that is, to impose a periodic 3D topography on the Li/ceramic electrolyte interface. For a given discharge current, the larger interfacial area should reduce the local current density, enabling higher discharge rates before voiding occurs. However, contouring also introduces heterogeneity in the current density distribution, and regions of higher local current are where voiding is most likely to begin. Contouring has been explored for mitigating dendrites on charging29,30,31, and we showed previously that it increases the charging current at which dendrites occur, by only a modest degree, less than 50%, too little to provide a viable solution to the problem of dendrites29. However, little or no attention has been given to the effect contouring might have on stripping and whether it can alleviate voiding. Given that voiding arises from the flux imbalance of Li and Li+ at the interface, a very different mechanism from dendrites on charging, the effect of contouring on discharge performance cannot be assumed to follow that seen for charging.Here we contour the Li/Li6PS5Cl interface by 3D templating and examine its effect on voiding during discharge. At 2 MPa and 30 °C, contouring increases the discharge current at which voiding commences tenfold, from 0.2 to 2 mA cm−2. In practice, cells are rarely discharged at a constant current throughout the whole discharge, therefore we also examined the effect of pulse discharge. Under pulsed conditions at 2 MPa, the contoured interface sustains currents of 3 mA cm−2 at 30 °C and 8 mA cm−2 at 60 °C. It also sustains a discharge sequence derived from the Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Procedure (WLTP), in which current peaks reach 9 mA cm−2, whereas a non-contoured interface fails. A full cell with an 80 µm contoured Li6PS5Cl electrolyte and a LiNi0.83Mn0.06Co0.11O2 composite cathode cycles stably at a discharge current of 6 mA cm−2 at 2 MPa and 60 °C, whereas the corresponding non-contoured cell fails during the second charge. Our findings show that contouring has a substantial effect on the discharge of solid-state batteries with lithium metal anodes and ceramic electrolytes, sustaining higher constant and pulsed discharge currents and completing the WLTP discharge sequence.Optimizing the contour geometryThe variation of current density across a contoured Li/solid electrolyte (SE) interface, and consequently the maximum local current density (where voids will form), depends on the topography of the interface. Previously, we calculated the current distribution for three topographies, frustums of square pyramids, egg box and square pyramids29 (Fig. 1a), and for the same applied discharge current, the maximum local current is lowest for the egg-box topography29 (Supplementary Fig. 1). High local currents occur at sudden changes in direction across the surface, that is, sharp corners, which the sinusoidal shape of the egg-box topography avoids. To measure the critical current of stripping (CCS) for the three topographies, 3D-printed polymer templates were pressed onto Argyrodite, Li6PS5Cl, powder in a die set, transferring the topography onto the Li6PS5Cl disc; the template was then removed, the solid electrolyte sintered and the lithium anode attached. The CCS was measured using three-electrode cells to avoid any influence from polarization at the counter electrode. Throughout this work, voiding was judged to have commenced when the voltage polarization grew by 2 mV during stripping (Supplementary Fig. 2). The CCS is highest for the egg-box topography (Fig. 1b), consistent with it having the lowest maximum local interfacial current in the calculated current density distributions (Supplementary Fig. 1). Therefore, as in our previous investigation of plating, the egg-box topography was considered further29.Fig. 1: Influence of different contoured Li/Li6PS5Cl interfaces on experimentally determined CCS.Full size imagea, X-ray computed tomography virtual cross sections of the Li/SE interface for frustums of square pyramids (top), egg box (middle) and square pyramids (bottom) with a peak height (H) of 25 µm and a peak separation (S) of 150 µm. b, Experimentally determined CCS for the three topographies and for a non-contoured interface. c, 3D-simulated egg-box interface. d, 3D colour-mapped plot showing the experimentally determined CCS for cells with egg-box-contoured Li/Li6PS5Cl interfaces for various combinations of peak H and peak S. The experimentally determined CCS for the non-contoured interface is 1.2 mA cm−2. The colour bar is aligned with the left axis for reference, green is high CCS and red low. The data were collected using three-electrode cells to avoid influence from the counter electrode, at 7 MPa stack pressure and 30 °C.The egg-box topography is parameterized by peak height (H) and peak separation (S) (Fig. 1c). The experimentally determined CCS for a range of egg-box topographies with varying H and S is shown in Fig. 1d. X-ray computed tomography (XCT) virtual cross sections of the egg-box interface with various combinations of H and S are shown in Supplementary Fig. 3. The highest CCS is observed for peaks that are low in height and close together. This is consistent with the modelling, described in Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. 4, the results of which are presented in Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 5 and discussed below.Fig. 2: Modelling for the egg-box-contoured interface with different peak heights and separations.Full size imagea–c, Calculated factors at the bottom of the troughs current density (a), pressure (b) and vacancy concentration (c) (note the inverted axis for vacancy concentration in c) for different combinations of peak height and separation at 1 mA cm−2 geometrical current density and 7 MPa applied stack pressure. d, Superposition of a, b and c, showing the overlapping region where all three factors mitigate void formation. e, Experimental determined critical current density of stripping for cells with egg-box-contoured Li/Li6PS5Cl interfaces for various combinations of peak height and peak separation showing that the optimum experimentally determined combinations of peak height and separation (small peaks close together) are in accord with the overlapping region from d. White and black dashed lines in a and c indicate the corresponding values for a non-contoured interface.Several factors may influence void formation at contoured interfaces, such as the local current density, pressure and Li flux. Although a comprehensive model of voiding is beyond the scope of the present work, we consider here how each of these factors is affected at the bottom of the troughs, where voids initiate across a range of contour dimensions. Compared with a flat interface, contouring increases the surface area and therefore reduces the overall current density (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Egg-box contours with small peak separation generally exhibit lower current density at the bottom of the troughs, reducing the driving force for void formation (Fig. 2a). Considering pressure, contoured surfaces that provide greater pressure gradients towards the bottom of the troughs will enhance creep and thus mitigate void formation (Supplementary Fig. 5b). This occurs when the pressures in the troughs are positive tending to zero. Consequently, all contoured combinations with lower trough pressures are expected to better resist void growth (Fig. 2b). Furthermore, the Li flux towards the troughs is enhanced at contoured compared with planar interfaces, analogous to how microelectrodes enhance mass transport in liquid electrochemistry32,33 (Supplementary Fig. 5c). The higher the flux towards the trough, the lower the concentration of vacancies at the base of the trough. As shown in Fig. 2c, greater flux to the trough (lower vacancy concentration) will occur for lower peak heights. Higher curvature enhances the local flux, but increasing peak height lengthens the diffusion path, which turns out to be the more important effect. Together these factors describe complementary aspects of the same process: the local current density sets the rate at which Li is removed at the trough, while pressure and Li flux determine the rate at which it is replenished from within the metal. The combined effect of current, pressure and Li flux in the troughs is shown by overlapping Fig. 2a–c in Fig. 2d. Only a subset of the contoured interfaces benefits from all three factors. They have small peaks relatively close together, consistent with the experimentally measured CCS results (Fig. 2e). Finer features could not be investigated because of the resolution limit of the 3D printing. At sufficiently small contour dimensions, approaching the scale of intrinsic electrolyte surface defects, the interfacial current distribution is expected to become dominated by stochastic surface defects rather than the controlled contour geometry. The lower limit of the contoured regime may therefore ultimately be set by the electrolyte surface defect population.Following these findings, an egg-box topography with a peak height of 5 µm and a peak separation of 30 µm was selected for further study.Constant current dischargeFigure 3 shows the results of cycling the contoured Li/SE interface under various conditions, with each case compared to the same conditions for the non-contoured interface. The non-contoured interface was formed by pressing Argyrodite electrolyte powder with flat 3D-printed polymer discs within a die set. Both contoured and non-contoured electrolytes exhibit similar defect densities near the electrolyte interface (Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Table 1). Li was pressed onto the contoured and non-contoured surfaces. In each case, the cell was first plated at 0.2 mA cm−2 for 1 mAh cm−2 and the cycled areal capacity was also 1 mAh cm−2. Figure 3a–c presents results collected at 30 °C. At a 7 MPa stack pressure, the contoured interface could sustain repeated cycles with discharge current densities of 4 mA cm−2 without appreciable polarization (<2 mV; Fig. 3a, left). By contrast, the non-contoured interface shows polarization during the first stripping, which increases on cycling indicating void accumulation (Fig. 3a, right). At 2 MPa and 30 °C, the highest discharge current that can be stably cycled using a contoured interface is 2 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3b, left). At atmospheric pressures (0.1 MPa), the highest discharge current possible is 0.5 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3c, left). At both 2 and 0.1 MPa, the non-contoured cells polarized drastically on the first stripping (Fig. 3b,c, right). Interestingly, remaining at atmospheric pressure but increasing the temperature to 60 °C raises the maximum discharge current density for the contoured interface to 4 mA cm−2, whereas the non-contoured interface shows very severe polarization on stripping (Fig. 3d). Increasing the pressure to 2 MPa at 60 °C then further elevates this to 6 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3e, left).Fig. 3: Li stripping at egg-box-contoured Li/SE interfaces compared with non-contoured interfaces under different applied pressures and temperatures.Full size imageWithin each panel, results for the egg-box-contoured interface (peak height of 5 µm, peak separation of 30 µm) are shown on the left and those for non-contoured interface on the right. a, Under 7 MPa at 30 °C with a stripping current of 4 mA cm−2. b, Under 2 MPa at 30 °C with a stripping current of 2 mA cm−2. c, Under 0.1 MPa at 30 °C with a stripping current of 0.5 mA cm−2. d, Under 0.1 MPa at 60 °C with a stripping current of 4 mA cm−2. e, Under 2 MPa at 60 °C with a stripping current of 6 mA cm−2. Cycling of the three-electrode Li/Li6PS5Cl cells was carried out using a low plating current of 0.2 mA cm−2 in all cases to avoid dendrites during plating. For all cells, an areal capacity of 1 mAh cm−2 is moved per half cycle.The results in Fig. 3 represent the maximum stripping currents for the contoured interfaces under each condition, as confirmed by Supplementary Fig. 7, which shows that any further increase in stripping current will result in appreciable polarization. Non-contoured interfaces can only cycle with a maximum discharge current density of 0.1 mA cm−2 at 2 MPa and 30 °C, and 0.3 mA cm−2 at 0.1 MPa and 60 °C without substantial polarization (Supplementary Fig. 8). Comparing Fig. 3 with Supplementary Fig. 8 shows that at low pressures contouring can enable an order of magnitude improvement in stable stripping current densities.Additionally, full cells with both contoured and non-contoured interfaces were constructed with a composite cathode consisting of LiNi0.83Mn0.06Co0.11O2, Li6PS5Cl and carbon nanofibres34 (see Methods for details). When discharging at 6 mA cm−2 under 2 MPa and 60 °C, the contoured full cell demonstrated stable cycling (Supplementary Fig. 9a), whereas the non-contoured full cell showed polarization during the first discharge and short circuit during the subsequent charge (Supplementary Fig. 9b). Wang et al. previously reported that voids can initiate when cycling at low current densities due to Li fatigue35. Cells with contoured Li/SE interfaces cycled under similar conditions show no clear signs of failure (Supplementary Fig. 10), which is consistent with the low calculated pressures at the bottom of the contoured troughs (where stripping currents are highest). Contouring does not change the intrinsic mechanical properties of lithium, but it does change the local stresses at the interface which drive fatigue (Fig. 2b).Pulse dischargeIn many applications, including automotive, cells undergo periods of constant current discharge, but they also have to sustain pulses of higher currents, for example, during acceleration. Pulse discharge is increasingly recognized as an important factor in evaluating solid-state batteries, as noted by Lee and Sakamoto36. Using open access information on typical drive cycles for passenger vehicles37, we extracted their average durations of acceleration and high speed (pulse) and the average durations of deceleration and idling (constant low current discharge) (Supplementary Table 2). Taking the case of the longest average pulse duration in Supplementary Table 2, we established a pulse-stripping protocol involving a pulse duration of 14 s, followed by a return to a lower discharge current of 0.2 mA cm−2 for 8 s (Fig. 4a). During the protocol, the pulse sequence is repeated until 1 mAh cm−2 is stripped, after which an equal amount of Li is plated back at 0.2 mA cm−2.Fig. 4: Pulsed stripping of egg-box-contoured Li/SE interfaces at different temperatures and pressures.Full size imagea, Schematic illustration of the pulse-stripping protocol which involves a pulse-stripping current lasting 14 s and a low current stripping current of 0.2 mA cm−2 lasting 8 s; the sequence is repeated until an areal capacity of 1 mAh cm−2 has been stripped. Following this protocol, the electrode is plated again at 0.2 mA cm−2 and an areal capacity of 1 mAh cm−2. Three-electrode cells were employed to avoid influence from the counter electrode. Before the pulse cycling, Li was plated to an areal capacity of 1 mAh cm−2. b–h, Results for the egg-box-contoured interface (peak height of 5 µm, peak separation of 30 µm) under various conditions: 2 MPa at 30 °C with a pulse-stripping current of 3 mA cm−2 (b). c,d, Magnified views of the first and 25th pulse-stripping sets in b, with an x-axis break between 370 and 1,450 s so that individual pulses can be seen more clearly. e,f, Voltage of each pulse as a function of time within the first (e) and 25th (f) pulse sets in b; from pulse 1 to pulse 82 within each set, the colours go from red to green. g, 2 MPa at 60 °C with a pulse-stripping current of 8 mA cm−2. h, 0.1 MPa at 60 °C with a pulse-stripping current of 5 mA cm−2.Figure 4b–h show the results of the pulse-stripping protocol for the contoured interface under various pressures and temperatures. At 2 MPa and 30 °C, a pulse discharge current of 3 mA cm−2 can be sustained for repeated cycles. Increasing the temperature to 60 °C enables an increase in pulse discharge current to 8 mA cm−2. When the pressure is reduced to atmospheric pressure (0.1 MPa), a pulse discharge current of 5 mA cm−2 can be sustained at 60 °C. These pulse discharge currents represent the maximum possible, as Supplementary Fig. 11 shows that higher pulse discharge currents lead to substantial polarization after several cycles.A comparison of Figs. 3 and 4 demonstrates that higher pulse discharge currents are possible compared to constant current discharge under identical pressures and temperatures. To understand why, the voltage profile of the first pulse set in Fig. 4b is shown in Fig. 4c, with the discharge curves for each pulse shown in Fig. 4e. There is some increase in polarization within each pulse and also from pulse to pulse within the set. During the first pulse, the polarization increased by 0.7 mV, and around 70% of this increase (0.46 mV) was retained at the start of the second pulse. Throughout the first pulse set, the polarization increases per pulse converge to around 0.3 mV, and the percentage retained between subsequent pulses reduces to less than 3%. As a result, the total growth in polarization across the first set is only around 1.7 mV from the start of the first pulse to the end of the final pulse. The final (25th) pulse set, expanded in Fig. 4d and Fig. 4f, shows similar changes in polarization, as seen across every pulse set in Fig. 4b. As can be seen in Supplementary Fig. 12, the same polarization behaviour was also observed for the cells in Fig. 4g,h.After 1 mAh cm−2 is stripped by a set of pulses, an equal amount of Li is plated back to the working electrode. Supplementary Fig. 13a–c show the initial voltages of each stripping pulse set corresponding to Fig. 4b,g,h, respectively. Notably, plating induces an almost complete return to the same polarization behaviour as observed initially. Across the cycling in Fig. 4, the average voltage difference retained between any two pulse sets did not exceed 0.1 mV.Overall, these observations are consistent with void formation occurring at the interface during a 14-s high current density stripping pulse, inducing polarization. During the 8-s intervals of low current stripping, Li transport in the anode towards the interface exceeds the Li stripping current, enabling a partial recovery of the contact loss. During plating after each set of pulses, the polarization almost fully returns to the value at the beginning of the first pulse from the previous pulse set, consistent with both Li transport within the anode and freshly plated Li filling the voids. When high discharge currents are only required for relatively short durations, with periods of lower current between, the accumulation of voiding and its more catastrophic effects are avoided, so that a solid-state cell may endure discharge currents in excess of the measured constant current CCS with negligible net growth in polarization.Having established the response to a pulse profile based on the longest average pulse duration in typical drive cycles, we next examined a complete standardized drive cycle, in which pulses of differing magnitude and duration occur within a single discharge sequence.Drive cycle assessmentThe WLTP is the most widely used drive cycle globally for regulatory compliance, emissions and range testing of passenger vehicles38,39,40 and is specifically designed to represent typical driving conditions that a passenger car would experience in real-world use. It comprises four phases, low, medium, high and extra-high speed, capturing typical driving behaviours from urban stop-and-go traffic to motorway driving. Using open-source data from Argonne National Laboratory’s electric vehicle testing project41, we used the measured current profile for an electric vehicle subject to the WLTP to derive a test protocol that reproduces the current densities experienced at the cell level. The WLTP speed profile and derived current profile are shown in Fig. 5a, with further details in Methods.Fig. 5: Comparison of the egg-box-contoured and non-contoured Li/SE interface based on the WLTP.Full size imagea, Vehicle speed profile of the WLTP, along with the corresponding current density at the cell level derived from an open-source electric vehicle testing database41. The WLTP current density profile was repeated ten times to achieve a total stripped areal capacity of 3.31 mAh cm−2. Subsequently, the cell was plated at 0.2 mA cm−2 for the same capacity. Before the WLTP drive cycles, an initial plating of 3.31 mAh cm−2 was performed. b–d, WLTP drive cycles for a three-electrode cell with an egg-box-contoured interface (peak height of 5 µm, peak separation of 30 µm) under 2 MPa and 60 °C. b, Voltage profiles during ten consecutive WLTP drive cycles with a slow plating current of 0.2 mA cm−2 between each set of discharges. c, Expanded view of the first WLTP drive cycle set of ten WLTP cycles. d, Detailed voltage profile of the first WLTP cycle within the set. e, WLTP drive cycles for a non-contoured three-electrode cell under 2 MPa and 60 °C. Inset, expanded view of the voltage profile during the first set of ten WLTP cycles.The WLTP drive cycle demands cell-level discharge current densities of up to ~2 mA cm−2 and pulse discharge current densities as high as 9 mA cm−2 with a total areal capacity of 0.331 mAh cm−2, corresponding to around 30 min of driving (Fig. 5a). To simulate extended operation, ten consecutive WLTP discharge current density profiles were concatenated, giving a total discharge areal capacity of 3.31 mAh cm−2, approximately five hours of driving. An equivalent amount of lithium was then plated back at 0.2 mA cm−2, allowing the WLTP discharge sequence to be repeated and the cell to be cycled. The cycling result for a three-electrode Li/Li6PS5Cl cell with an egg-box-contoured interface under 2 MPa at 60 °C is shown in Fig. 5b. During the first WLTP discharge sequence, the contoured interface enabled ten consecutive WLTP cycles without appreciable polarization (<2 mV; Fig. 5c). Figure 5d shows the first WLTP cycle within the first set, which corresponds to the current density profile in Fig. 5a. Across 75 cycles, the total polarization for the contoured cell remained below 2 mV (Fig. 5b). By contrast, the non-contoured interface showed an increase in polarization of around 250 mV during the first WLTP discharge sequence (the inset of Fig. 5e) and polarized to 5 V before completing the second cycle (Fig. 5e).Notably, the maximum pulse current density within the WLTP sequence, 9 mA cm−2 exceeded the maximum pulse discharge current in Fig. 4g of 8 mA cm−2. The ability of the contoured cell to withstand the higher currents under the WLTP drive cycle is attributed to the inherently shorter pulse durations and longer recovery intervals in the WLTP compared with the protocols used in Fig. 4. To illustrate this more directly, pulse stripping with a 9 mA cm−2 pulse discharge current and an equivalent areal capacity of 3.31 mAh cm−2 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 14, showing how large polarization develops after eight cycles. Beyond pure Li metal, a Li-rich Ag alloy (0.5% Ag) with faster Li diffusivity42,43 was subject to the same pulse-stripping cycling. The results show enhanced performance and stable pulse stripping for 20 cycles (Supplementary Fig. 15), consistent with the role of Li flux in the anode in mitigating void formation.In situ XCT shows no obvious structural change after one complete WLTP drive cycle (Supplementary Fig. 16), indicating that the contoured interface retains its original morphology after cycling, and this structure is maintained after 15 WLTP drive cycle sets (Supplementary Fig. 17).While the results of the constant current cycling in Fig. 3 cannot be used to predict precisely the results for the WLTP protocol in Fig. 5, it is possible to identify thresholds of constant current cycling that accord with the WLTP protocol. A contoured cell that can undergo stable cycling up to a stripping current of 6 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3e, left) can also complete the WLTP drive cycle at the same conditions of 2 MPa and 60 °C. In contrast, although stable constant current stripping was observed at 4 mA cm−2 under the conditions of 7 MPa at 30 °C and 0.1 MPa at 60 °C (Fig. 3a,d, left), these cells exhibited severe polarization after tens of cycles under the WLTP protocol (Supplementary Fig. 18a,b). Overall, stable cycling at 6 mA cm−2, 2 MPa and 60 °C provides a benchmark for completing the WLTP drive cycle and an approximate conversion between constant current stripping and the WLTP protocol.Overall, while non-contoured cells cannot survive a single WLTP discharge sequence, an egg-box-contoured Li/Li6PS5Cl cell can repeatedly sustain multiple concatenated WLTP drive cycles with a total areal capacity of 3.31 mAh cm−2 without any appreciable polarization under 2 MPa and 60 °C.Implications of contouring on energy densityContouring the lithium metal/ceramic electrolyte interface inevitably reduces the volumetric energy density compared with a non-contoured interface. Figure 6 shows a typical estimate of the volumetric energy density for a solid-state battery with a non-contoured lithium anode (based on a composite cathode thickness25 of 120 µm, a solid electrolyte thickness44,45 of 20 µm and Al and Cu current collectors46,47 each 10-µm thick) and the degree to which contouring reduces it. The details of the structure with an egg-box-contoured interface are provided in Supplementary Fig. 19 and Supplementary Note 2. The combination of a peak height of 5 µm and a peak separation of 30 µm, as used in this work, reduces the volumetric energy density by only 5% while substantially increasing the discharge rate capabilities of the cell. Greater peak heights and separations begin to markedly compromise the volumetric energy density.Fig. 6: The effect of egg-box-contoured interfaces on the volumetric energy density of Li metal anode solid-state batteries.Full size imageTheoretical volumetric energy densities are presented for all-solid-state batteries with a non-contoured interface, H5S30 egg box (peak height of 5 µm, peak separation of 30 µm) and H25S150 egg-box-contoured interfaces. For comparison, the theoretical volumetric energy density of state-of-the-art lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with a liquid electrolyte is shown, taken from refs. 44,47.To assess the effect of contouring in a more practical cell format, a full cell was constructed comprising a thin contoured Li6PS5Cl solid electrolyte and a composite cathode of LiNi0.83Mn0.06Co0.11O2, Li6PS5Cl and carbon nanofibres. As shown in Fig. 7a the topography of the contoured interface is retained after warm isostatic pressing. This cell exhibits stable cycling at 6 mA cm−2 on discharge and 0.5 mA cm−2 on charge under 2 MPa and 60 °C, whereas the corresponding non-contoured cell fails during the second charge (Fig. 7b–d).Fig. 7: Comparison of full cells with thin contoured and non-contoured solid electrolytes, showing stable cycling for the contoured electrolyte.Full size imagea, X-ray computed tomography virtual cross-section for a full cell with ~120-μm-thick composite cathode, composed of LiNi0.83Mn0.06Co0.11O2, Li6PS5Cl and carbon nanofibres, an ~80-μm-thick contoured Li6PS5Cl solid electrolyte and lithium metal anode. b,c, Load curves for full cells with the egg-box-contoured thin solid electrolyte (shown in a) (b); a non-contoured thin solid electrolyte, both under 2 MPa at 60 °C (c). The discharge current density is 6 mA cm−2 and the charge current density is 0.5 mA cm−2, with an areal capacity of 4 mAh cm−2. d, Corresponding specific discharge capacity and coulombic efficiency for the cell in b.DiscussionContouring the interface between the lithium metal anode and ceramic electrolyte can substantially enhance the discharge currents that are possible without encountering polarization and voiding at the interface. An egg-box-contoured topography with peak height and separation of 5 and 30 µm, respectively, at the Li/Li6PS5Cl interface, increases the discharge current at which voiding commences tenfold over a non-contoured interface, from 0.2 to 2 mA cm−2 when cycled under 2 MPa stack pressure at 30 °C. Even higher discharge currents can be sustained if they are pulsed. Contoured cells under 2 MPa stack pressure can sustain pulsed currents of 3 mA cm−2 at 30 °C and 8 mA cm−2 at 60 °C.The WLTP is designed to represent typical driving conditions that a passenger car would experience in real-world use. By translating the WLTP drive cycle into a discharge current profile at cell level, we showed that the WLTP could be sustained at 2 MPa stack pressure and 60 °C, involving discharge currents as high as 9 mA cm−2. In contrast, a non-contoured interface polarizes to 5 V before completing two cycles of the WLTP protocol under the same conditions. These results further reinforce the importance of mitigating voiding on discharge and dendrites on charge to enable Li anode cells capable of satisfying driving conditions.Recognizing the role of Li flux in the anode as a contributory factor to mitigate voiding, we also examined a contoured interface with a Li-Ag alloy anode. This exhibited yet higher discharge currents, in accord with the higher Li flux, and the same approach could be extended to other alloy anodes with fast Li transport19,20. In our previous paper29, examining the effect of contouring the interface on dendrite formation on charging, we showed it can only improve charging currents by an additional 50% at most. Contouring to mitigate voiding and polarization on discharge could therefore be combined with strategies to mitigate dendrites on charging25,48,49. Developing a predictive model of void formation at contoured interfaces will be important for future work. Further work should also focus on implementing similar contoured interfaces on larger format solid-state cells with thin electrolytes using scalable techniques such as stamping or laser etching. The results presented here serve to demonstrate the potential value of contouring the Li/SE interface in raising discharge currents to practically relevant levels.MethodsFabrication of 3D templatesThe egg-box surface, \(f(x,y)\), was generated by sweeping a cosine wave along the trajectory of another identical, perpendicular cosine wave, as defined in equation (1), where \(H\) is the peak height (amplitude) and \(S\) is the peak separation (wavelength).$$f\;\left(x,y\right)=H\cos \left(\displaystyle\frac{2\pi}S\times x\right)+H\cos \left(\displaystyle\frac{2\pi}S\times y\right)$$
(1)
The 3D polymer templates were fabricated with a contoured side defined by \(f(x,y)\) and a non-contoured opposing side, with a diameter of 5 mm. The 3D template print files were processed using NanoWrite (Nanoscribe), with a slicing distance of 1 µm, a hatching distance of 0.5 µm and a layer-by-layer approach, employing a block size of 300 µm \(\times\) 300 µm to generate the printing trajectory. The 3D templates were then printed using a high-resolution commercial 3D printer (Nanoscribe Photonic Professional GT) with the Dip-in laser lithography printing configuration, a 25×/0.8 (objective/numerical aperture) lens and IP-S (Nanoscribe) resin. After printing, the template was washed with propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate (≥ 99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich) to remove excess unpolymerized resin, followed by rinsing with isopropanol (≥ 99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich). The cleaned template was then vacuum dried overnight before being used in an argon-filled glovebox.Fabrication of Li6PS5Cl solid electrolyte discsFor contoured electrolytes, 30 mg of Li6PS5Cl (AMPCERA) powder with an average particle size of 1 µm was loaded into a 5-mm die with the 3D template. A uniaxial pressure of 400 MPa was applied to imprint the contoured surface of the 3D template onto the Li6PS5Cl disc while densifying the electrolyte to a thickness of approximately 1 mm. The 3D template was removed from the Li6PS5Cl disc after pressing. For the non-contoured Li6PS5Cl discs, the interface was formed by pressing the Argyrodite electrolyte powder with flat 3D-printed polymer discs within a die set. In both the contoured and non-contoured cases, the pressed Li6PS5Cl discs were heat treated in a muffle furnace at 300 °C for 30 min to enhance the ionic conductivity. The improvement in discharge performance is independent of the heat treatment, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 20, which shows a non-sintered contoured electrolyte can withstand the WLTP drive cycle without appreciable polarization. No noticeable differences in surface defects and no notable mechanical damage occurs on either the contoured or non-contoured surfaces (Supplementary Fig. 21). All procedures were conducted in an argon-filled glovebox (O2 and H2O < 1 ppm).Three-electrode cell preparationThe three-electrode cells were constructed using Li metal for the working, counter and reference electrodes. One-mm, 0.5-mm and 5-mm Li discs were used as the working, reference and counter electrodes, respectively. The working and reference were located on one surface of the disc and the counter on the other with an insulating polymer to ensure isolation between the working and reference electrodes. The three-electrode cells were then encapsulated in Mylar pouches with stainless steel as the current collector. Before electrochemical measurements, all cells underwent heat treatment at 80 °C under 7 MPa to enable intimate interfacial contact. The contact angles of molten Li on the Li6PS5Cl surface are similar for both the contoured and non-contoured interfaces (Supplementary Fig. 22).Preparation of Li-Ag alloy anodeAg foil (Goodfellow, 99.99%) and Li metal were weighted to the desired atomic ratio and loaded into a BN crucible in an argon-filled glovebox (O2 and H2O < 1 ppm). The loaded crucible was heated to 500 °C and held for 2 h with gentle agitation. After the dwell, the melt was cooled to room temperature to obtain a solid Li-Ag ingot.Measurements of the critical current density of strippingThe critical current density for stripping (CCS), constant current and pulse cycling were conducted using the Gamry 1010E potentiostat. The CCS was determined by slow plating at 0.2 mA cm−2 and stripping at 0.2 mA cm−2 with an areal capacity of 0.2 mAh cm−2. For subsequent cycles, the stripping current was increased by a step of 0.2 mA cm−2 each cycle, while the plating current remained at 0.2 mA cm−2. To detect the early onset of voiding, we used a low but consistently observable polarization increase of 2 mV to determine the CCS, as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 2.Full cellThe composite cathode, consisting of LiNi0.83Mn0.06Co0.11O2 (MSE Supplies), Li6PS5Cl and carbon nanofibres (Sigma-Aldrich) in a weight ratio of 75:22:3, was prepared by mixing the powders with a pestle and mortar. A cathode composite powder of 5.2 mg, together with 30 mg of Li6PS5Cl and a 3D-printed template, was subsequently loaded into a 5-mm die. A uniaxial pressure of 400 MPa was then applied to form the full cell with either a contoured or a non-contoured anode. The 3D-printed template was removed from the full cell disc after pressing, and a 5-mm Li metal disc was subsequently pressed onto the anode side. The thin contoured full cell was prepared using 2.4 mg of Li6PS5Cl with a 3D-printed template and 5.2 mg of composite cathode. The cell was pre-densified in a 5-mm die set at 50 MPa, followed by warm isostatic pressing at 450 MPa and 80 °C for 30 mins. A 5-mm Li metal disc was then pressed onto the anode cell. The assembled full cells were sealed in pouches using stainless steel current collectors for both the cathode and anode. The cut-off voltages for charge and discharge were set to 4.25 V and 2.5 V, respectively.
